prose.title: The Losers Who Started Ghosts
prose.dek: Every man who lost a game he could have won had a starter who never took the field, and the title is down to two housemates.

paragraphs: Puka Nacua caught everything thrown near him for Shawn Blake -- {{f.star.line}} -- in a game that leads nowhere at all. He had averaged {{f.star.prior_avg}} coming into the round and had never cleared {{f.star.prior_best}} in a week all season. Blake won anyway. He is not playing for the title and Nacua's afternoon did not change that, which is the cruellest sentence in this entire recap.

Only one owner beat every team in the league this week: {{f.week.perfect}}. Jared Goff supplied {{f.player.jared-goff.score}} of it and Christian McCaffrey another {{f.player.christian-mccaffrey.score}}, and the two of them together turned a playoff game into a demolition. Martel is one of two men left alive for the title.

The other is Brian Cutting, who did it with the whole receiving corps rather than one act. Chris Olave went for {{f.player.chris-olave.score}}, Ashton Jeanty added {{f.player.ashton-jeanty.score}}, and Drake Maye chipped in {{f.player.drake-maye.score}} on top. Bear Dunn had offered his encouragement before any of it happened.

Down the other end, the only owner to lose to every single team in the field was {{f.week.winless}}, which is a hard thing to do in a week where the scoring was this generous. The wire produced {{f.wire.adds}} adds and the best of them, {{f.wire.best_add}}, spent the round on Eric Martel's bench while Martel lost his season. Some of the losers were simply beaten. The rest of them handed it over.

captions.t.performers: The quarterbacks ran the top of it again, and mostly for owners who won.
captions.t.pickups: Eric Martel found the week's best free agent and watched him from the bench.

paragraphs: Ryan Bousquet started a defensive tackle who never took a snap -- {{f.dnp.0001}}. Keith Creelman did the same with a defensive end, {{f.dnp.0008}}. Brian Cross doubled up: his lineup held {{f.dnp.0006}}, and neither of them played a down.

Those are exactly the {{f.week.self_inflicted}} losers who had a winning lineup available and did not put it on the field. The other {{f.week.outgunned}} -- Eric Martel, Bear Dunn, Derrick Whitman -- could have played a flawless card and still gone home. It holds all six ways.

Bousquet's bench was the loudest of it. He had {{f.burn.benched}} sitting there, and Stafford outscored the quarterback he actually started by more than the game was decided by; the verdict is that {{f.burn.verdict}}. Creelman's swing and Eric Martel's were the other kind entirely -- the man with the better season average started and had a bad day, which is variance and not a decision anybody should be mocked for.

gameNotes.g.1: Eric Martel arrived with the better record and left with a card he could not have improved -- his best available lineup, {{f.team.0005.best_available}}, loses this game too. Cutting has been the stronger team inside their shared bracket all year and he made it look procedural, winning by {{f.game.01.margin}}. Martel's season is over on merit rather than on error, which is the version nobody enjoys.
gameNotes.g.2: Bear Dunn beat most of the league this week -- {{f.team.0009.week_allplay}} against the field -- and ran into the one team that beat all of it. His perfect lineup, {{f.team.0009.best_available}}, is not in the neighbourhood of what Josh Martel put up, and the margin was {{f.game.02.margin_rank}}. The division he has controlled all season buys him precisely nothing from here.
gameNotes.g.3: Ryan Bousquet is the one man knocked out of the title race this round who could have prevented it himself: {{f.team.0001.best_available}} was on his roster and it beats what Blake scored. His best starter, {{f.team.0001.best_player}}, was superb and irrelevant, because {{f.team.0001.left_on_bench}} never got into the game. Blake, who cannot win the title either, played the better lineup of two teams that both had one available.
gameNotes.g.4: Brian Cross got the best individual performance on the field and lost by {{f.game.04.margin}}, which is the smallest margin of the round. Two of his starters never played, and his best available card, {{f.team.0006.best_available}}, clears what Mannila actually scored. Mannila needed nothing more than a normal week -- he finished within a whisker of his own average, {{f.team.0011.vs_avg}} -- and it was enough to pull him clear of the cellar fight.
gameNotes.g.5: Klingenberg and Creelman came in with identical all-play records and produced the ugliest game of the round, which at least felt fair. Creelman finished {{f.team.0008.vs_avg}} against his own average with a defensive end in his lineup who never played, and his best card, {{f.team.0008.best_available}}, wins this. The Kenneth Walker benching looks damning and isn't -- the man who started had the better season behind him -- so save the abuse for the starter who wasn't there.
gameNotes.g.6: Derrick Whitman scored {{f.team.0002.score}} and lost to the entire league on the way through, and his flawless lineup, {{f.team.0002.best_available}}, still does not win this. That is not a management failure, it is a roster that has run out of football players. Gerardi won by {{f.game.06.margin}} and remains in cellar danger regardless, which tells you how deep the hole was before he climbed.

captions.t.burns: Read the verdict column before you laugh at anybody.

paragraphs: Brian Cutting and Josh Martel are the last two men who can still win this thing, and they share a division. Cutting is its leader of record, {{f.div.legion-of-boom.leader}}, on a division mark Martel has not matched; Martel has the heavier scoring behind him. Neither of them has the best won-lost record in the league and neither of them cares.

Bear Dunn owns DOG POUND 4 LIFE at {{f.div.dog-pound-4-life.leader}} and owns nothing else that matters now. Eric Martel took ICE UP SON! at {{f.div.ice-up-son.leader}} and was knocked out by a team that finished behind him in the win column. Bousquet and Blake are in the same room with the same problem: still in the championship bracket, no longer able to win it. None of it maps to record.

Shawn Blake leads MAKE IT RAIN at {{f.div.make-it-rain.leader}}, a record that should not lead a fantasy division and does, because the four winners get in and the rest of the field is sorted by how often you beat everybody. That is how a man can be {{f.team.0012.week_allplay}} against the field this week, as Klingenberg was, and still be the one who advanced.

The cellar fight is where the real menace is. Creelman, Cross, Gerardi and Whitman are all {{f.team.0002.bracket}}, and Whitman has now given the field a week it can build a whole offseason of jokes on. Klingenberg and Mannila are {{f.team.0011.bracket}}, having done nothing especially impressive except win when it counted, which is the entire skill. Next round settles a champion and, more expensively, a last place.

captions.t.standings: The record column and the seeding argument are not the same argument, and this week proved it twice.
